lead: Big models predict well but cost memory, battery and latency. Compression keeps most of the accuracy in a much smaller package. Three standard routes are distillation (a small student model learns from a large teacher), quantization (weights and activations use fewer bits, usually INT8 instead of FP32) and pruning (small or structured weights are removed). You meet this when a phone runs a speech recogniser offline, when a startup serves a language model on one GPU, or when a booking site must answer many users cheaply.
prereq: You need: 5.3 and 5.4 for model structure and size, and Unit 2 for regularization and fine-tuning.

sections.h3: Distillation: soft targets at a temperature

blocks.text: Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. The teacher's softmax gives a probability for every class, not just the true label. A picture of a cat may get 0.80 cat, 0.15 dog and 0.05 fox, which tells the student that cat and dog are similar. A one-hot label hides that information.

blocks.where: L is the student loss; y is the true one-hot label; p_s is the student's normal softmax output; p_t^T = softmax(z_t/T) and p_s^T = softmax(z_s/T) are softened outputs from teacher logits z_t and student logits z_s; T > 0 is the temperature; α in [0,1] weights the two terms; CE is cross-entropy; KL is Kullback–Leibler divergence.

blocks.text: Temperature T > 1 softens the distribution: rare classes get visible probability. The T² factor keeps the gradient scale similar when T changes. α balances the hard-label loss and the imitation loss. Use T = 1 and the student alone at inference.

items: Run each training input through the teacher at temperature T and keep the soft outputs.
Train the student on the same inputs with the combined loss L.
Set T = 1 and deploy only the student.

blocks.text: Distillation is common when a large BERT-style encoder must become a small encoder for a phone, or when a large chat model must become a smaller chat model.

Quantization maps real numbers to low-precision integers. A weight x is stored as an integer code q, and the model computes with q. The scale s and zero point z are chosen so the important range fits.
q = clamp(round(x/s) + z, q_min, q_max),   x̂ = s(q − z)
blocks.where: x is the real value; q is the stored integer code; s is the scale (real units per integer step); z is the integer zero point; q_min and q_max are the integer limits, for example −127 and 127 for symmetric INT8; x̂ is the dequantized value.

blocks.text: Clamp keeps q inside the chosen integer range. For symmetric INT8, z = 0 and q lies in [−127, 127]. For asymmetric, z maps real zero to an integer, so zero padding stays zero.

FP16 and BF16 are the easy middle step: half the memory of FP32, little accuracy loss. INT8 cuts memory four times and often speeds inference. Post-training quantization (PTQ) calibrates s and z on a small sample and needs no retraining. Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates rounding during training and usually gives better accuracy. Use per-channel scales for convolution and linear layers when one channel has an outlier.
For a tensor, per-tensor uses one s and z for all values; per-channel uses one pair per output channel. A single outlier weight can stretch a per-tensor scale and crush small values into zero.

Pruning removes weights. Magnitude pruning deletes weights with |w| below a threshold. Unstructured pruning gives a sparse matrix; it saves memory but ordinary hardware rarely speeds up because the nonzeros are irregular. Structured pruning removes whole channels, filters or attention heads; the result is a dense smaller model that runs fast on ordinary GPUs and phones.

Prune iteratively: train, remove a small fraction, fine-tune, repeat. Fine-tuning after each round recovers accuracy. The lottery-ticket idea says a sparse subnetwork found early can sometimes retrain to full accuracy; treat it as a research guide, not a deployment promise.

Deployment is the end point. Export the compressed model to TFLite for mobile or ONNX Runtime for servers, then check accuracy and latency on the target device. A common pipeline uses all three routes: distill a large teacher, quantize the student, prune structured blocks, and fine-tune once more.

examples.question: Quantize the four weights [−0.9, 0.1, 0.7, 0.0] to symmetric INT8 with zero point z = 0 and range [−127, 127]. Find s, each integer code q, each dequantized value x̂, the largest error, and the storage saving.
steps: For x = 0.0: x/s = 0.0, round to q = 0. Dequantize: x̂ = 0 × 0.0070866 = 0.000. Error = 0.0000.
Largest error = 0.0016. FP32 storage = 4 × 32 = 128 bits. INT8 storage = 4 × 8 = 32 bits. Saving = 128 / 32 = 4×.
examples.answer: The INT8 codes are [−127, 14, 99, 0], dequantized values are [−0.900, 0.0992, 0.7016, 0.0000], the largest error is 0.0016, and storage falls 4× from 128 bits to 32 bits.
examples.check:
s = 0.9 / 127
w = [-0.9, 0.1, 0.7, 0.0]
q = [round(x / s) for x in w]
dq = [x * s for x in q]
for code in q:
    print(code)
for value in dq:
    print(round(value, 4))
print(round(max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(w, dq)), 4))
print(round((4 * 32) / (4 * 8), 1))

traps: A single outlier weight can wreck a per-tensor scale: small weights round to zero. Check per-channel scales or clip the range.
Pruning without fine-tuning loses accuracy. Sparsity does not speed up ordinary hardware unless the structure is regular, such as whole channels or heads.
In distillation, forget the T² factor and the gradient scale changes; forget T = 1 at inference and the student stays softened.
INT8 saves 4× memory, not always 4× time. Activation conversions, memory bandwidth and kernels decide the real speedup.
The zero point is not always 0. Symmetric quantization uses z = 0; asymmetric quantization needs z to map real zero correctly.

quiz.q: What does the temperature T do in distillation?
quiz.a: T > 1 softens the teacher and student softmax distributions, making rare-class probabilities visible. At inference the student uses T = 1.

quiz.q: Why are soft targets more informative than one-hot labels?
quiz.a: Soft targets give a probability for every class. They show which classes are similar, for example cat 0.80 and dog 0.15. A one-hot label gives only the true class.

quiz.q: A weight 0.4 is quantized with s = 0.01 and z = 0. Give q and the dequantized value.
A model has 1,000,000 FP32 weights. What is the INT8 memory in MB, and what is the saving? Use 32 bits for FP32 and 8 bits for INT8.
One weight is 10 while most weights lie in [−1, 1]. Why can per-tensor INT8 hurt accuracy?
quiz.a: The large value sets s from the maximum absolute value. With s based on 10, a step is large, so weights near 0.1 or 0.01 round to zero or very few levels. Per-channel scales or clipping reduce this damage.

quiz.q: Why does 90% unstructured sparsity not guarantee a 10× speedup?
quiz.a: The remaining weights are scattered irregularly. Dense hardware and libraries cannot skip them efficiently without sparse kernels, so memory may fall but time may not.

quiz.q: What is the difference between post-training quantization and quantization-aware training?
quiz.a: PTQ quantizes an already trained model using calibration data. QAT simulates rounding during training so the model learns to tolerate quantization, usually giving better accuracy.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production stacks combine all three routes: distill a large teacher, quantize the student, prune structured blocks, then export to TFLite or ONNX Runtime. Newer work uses 4-bit and 2-bit quantization, activation-aware scaling and sparsity-aware kernels. Search terms: knowledge distillation, INT8 quantization scale and zero point, magnitude pruning, lottery ticket hypothesis, quantization-aware training.
